strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/3e9153058f4045ef9df7f49bed12a649/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important practical observation: MIP solvers may find a high-quality incumbent substantially earlier than they can certify it. Learning a distribution-specific stopping rule is potentially useful in repeated-solve settings.

Applying conformal calibration to solver trajectories is a conceptually appealing extension of prior learning-to-optimize and conformal-optimization work. The distinction between accelerating the search and terminating an otherwise standard solver early is clearly motivated.

The experiments span six benchmark families, two solvers, and both synthetic and real-data-derived problem families. For CP-GRB, the reported runtime reductions are often large—for example, 431.8 to 96.2 seconds on OTS and 221.0 to 11.7 seconds on MIS.

The paper is generally organized clearly, and the limitations section honestly identifies the substantial offline cost, restriction to already-solvable instance distributions, variable speedup across families, and vulnerability to distribution shift.

The method leaves the underlying solver and feasibility machinery intact and uses relatively inexpensive trajectory features, which could make deployment practical once a sufficiently representative calibration distribution is available. No immediate research-ethics concern is evident.
weaknesses: The central 95% guarantee is not established as written. Lemma 4.2 has an off-by-one rank error: if the new observation has overall rank c+1−n, removing it makes the calibration order statistic one position larger, so that rank does not imply Z_{c+1}≥Z_[c+1−n]. The usual bound here is n/(c+1), consistent with Theorem 4.1's statement, not (n+1)/(c+1) as claimed by the lemma and proof. Section 4.1 nevertheless selects n using (n+1)/(c+1)≥1−α. With c=100 and n=95 this only supports 95/101≈94.1%, and with c=28 and n=27 only 27/29≈93.1%, rather than 95%. This directly invalidates the headline calibration prescription, though it appears repairable by using a more conservative order statistic.

The mathematical notation is materially inconsistent. Section 3 defines gθ(t) as the already normalized true optimality gap, but Section 5 defines s(θ,κ)=[gθ(τ̂κ(θ))−z*(θ)]/|z*(θ)|, which subtracts an objective value from a dimensionless gap. Sections 4.2 and 6 also alternate between g and ĝ for the predictor, while training it on the unnormalized quantity U−z* but describing it as the true optimality gap. These issues make several stated guarantees and the exact implemented target ambiguous.

The sample-conditional results are not rigorously proved. Theorem 5.2 applies a concentration statement to P̂ε and Pε after κ has been selected from the same calibration sample without establishing the required uniform bound over κ. A nested-class/DKW argument may repair this, but the provided proof does not. Theorem 5.1 similarly takes a supremum over u after invoking a VC bound stated only for each fixed u, and its theorem statement drops the factor √2 appearing in its own proof.

The empirical evidence does not consistently support the advertised 95% success claim at ε=0.1%. CP-GRB reaches only 88% correctness on MVC, while CP-COPT reaches 85% on GISP, 78.6% on OTS, 80% on MMCN, and 91% on MIS. Finite test variation alone can occur under marginal coverage, but the paper neither reports confidence intervals nor analyzes these substantial shortfalls. Figure 4 instead evaluates the looser 2ε=0.2% tolerance, despite the surrounding text describing ε-optimality, which further obscures validation of the main claim.

The baselines are inadequate to establish that the learned predictor is responsible for the gain. Besides exact solver termination, the only early-stopping baselines terminate after one or three incumbents and perform predictably poorly. Missing comparisons include a calibration-only fixed-time rule, native-gap or trajectory heuristics, a simple non-neural predictor, an oracle incumbent-attainment time, and the most closely related learned/conformal suboptimality methods. There are also no ablations of the LSTM, features, weighting, rolling minimum, calibration size, or distribution shift.

The reported speedup excludes the expensive requirement to solve 800 training instances plus calibration instances to obtain optimal labels. That amortization may be appropriate for repeated solves, but the paper does not quantify preprocessing compute, the break-even number of deployments, callback/inference overhead, or sensitivity to hardware and solver nondeterminism. Disabling presolve also weakens the relevance of comparisons to production solver configurations.

Reproducibility is poor. The sentence claiming that code is available ends with a blank link. Important details are missing, including learning rate, batch construction, epochs or stopping rule, random seeds, feature normalization, solver and library versions, callback sampling frequency δ, handling of y=0 in the 1/y loss weight, exact κ computation, and trained configurations for each solver. Commercial-solver dependencies further increase the need for executable artifacts.

Presentation and data-quality problems reduce confidence: the appendix contains a spurious “Maximum vertex capacity” table that exactly duplicates the MVC results; the paper alternates among MMCNDP, MMCN-medium-BI, and MMCN; the abstract says five families although six are evaluated; and several claims conflate marginal conformal coverage with a guarantee that at least 95% of a finite test set will be correct.

The originality is useful but moderate rather than transformative: conformal control of suboptimality for parametric MIPs is already represented by Clarke and Stellato (2025), and the new element is chiefly applying a calibrated score as an online termination rule. The related-work discussion does not provide enough technical comparison to isolate what is genuinely new.

The limitations discussion is candid but incomplete for high-stakes uses. Since a wrong early stop can affect power, transportation, or control decisions, the paper should discuss abstention or fallback mechanisms, monitoring for distribution shift, and the fact that marginal coverage does not protect every subgroup or individual instance. These concerns are not an ethical violation, but they matter for responsible deployment.

strengths: The core idea is useful: learning when a MIP incumbent is already near-optimal could avoid the often substantial time spent certifying optimality.

The evaluation covers six problem families and two commercial solvers, with separate training, calibration, and test sets and detailed tabular results. Several Gurobi experiments show large runtime reductions while retaining good average solution quality.
Calibrating a stopping rule rather than trusting raw neural predictions is conceptually appealing, and a corrected conformal construction could provide predictor-agnostic marginal guarantees.

The paper openly discusses important limitations, including expensive training-label generation, restriction to already-solvable problem families, heterogeneous speedups, and sensitivity to distribution shift. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.

The manuscript is generally organized and motivates the practical problem clearly. weaknesses: Soundness: the central conformal derivation contains an off-by-one error. Lemma 4.2 claims P[Z_{c+1} >= Z_[c+1-n]] >= (n+1)/(c+1), whereas for continuous iid variables the probability is n/(c+1). The rank implication in its proof is false. Although Theorem 4.1 states the n/(c+1) bound, its proof and the calibration prescription use (n+1)/(c+1). Thus the prescribed choice of n does not establish the advertised 1-alpha guarantee: for c=100 and alpha=0.05 it permits n=95, giving only 95/101, and for c=28 it permits n=27, giving only 27/29.

Soundness: the sample-conditional analysis is not rigorous as written. In Theorem 5.1, a VC bound established separately for each fixed u is placed under a supremum over all u without a uniform argument over u. Theorem 5.2 similarly applies a concentration statement directly to a threshold selected using the same calibration sample without explicitly establishing the required uniform empirical-process result.

Soundness and presentation: key definitions are inconsistent. The true gap is initially relative, while the training target is the absolute quantity U-z*. Section 5 then defines suboptimality using g_theta(t)-z*, which is dimensionally inconsistent with the earlier definition of g. Section 4 uses a bound-squashed predictor, whereas the experimental section states that the predictor is simply h(X). Moreover, h is declared nonnegative, which would restrict the sigmoid factor to at least one half of U-L.

Soundness: the proposed weight w proportional to 1/(U-z*) is undefined when the incumbent is optimal—the regime emphasized by the paper—and no clipping or regularization is specified. The continuous-time loss, discretized loss, and callback-sampled implementation also do not align clearly.

Evaluation: the reported correctness rates do not consistently realize the nominal 95% target. Examples include 88% for CP-GRB on MVC and 85%, 78.6%, 80%, and 91% for CP-COPT on several families. Since marginal conformal coverage is not reliably assessed by one calibration split, repeated calibration/test splits with uncertainty estimates are needed.

Evaluation and significance: baselines are limited to exact solving and extremely weak 'stop after 1/3 solutions' rules. There is no comparison with stronger learned stopping, prediction-bound, or solver-tuning alternatives; no predictor/calibration ablation; and no sensitivity analysis for training size, calibration size, alpha, or distribution shift. Disabling presolve and imposing one thread and 1 GB of memory further limits the relevance of the speedups to standard solver use.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the promised code link is blank. Important details are missing, including data splits/seeds, optimizer hyperparameters, sequence sampling and padding, treatment of zero loss weights, exact conformal quantile/tie handling, solver versions and parameters, and inference/callback overhead.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies: the abstract says five families while six are evaluated; Figure 4 evaluates 2epsilon=0.2% while the surrounding text describes epsilon-optimality; the stated covariates differ between the method and experiment sections; and the MVC results are duplicated under the erroneous heading 'Maximum vertex capacity.'

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional. Applying conformal calibration to an online solver stopping threshold is a plausible new combination, but it is close to prior conformal suboptimality certification and learned MIP heuristics. The paper does not sufficiently isolate what is technically new beyond that combination.

Overall, the potentially useful idea does not compensate for the invalid derivation of the headline guarantee, inconsistent formalization, and insufficiently reproducible evaluation. These are central rather than cosmetic issues and prevent acceptance in the current form.

strengths: Originality/significance: Learning a solver-state-dependent stopping rule and calibrating it with conformal prediction is a compelling direction. It targets the practically important gap between finding a good incumbent and certifying optimality, and differs meaningfully from work that learns branching, cuts, or primal heuristics.

Soundness—positive aspects: The train/calibrate/test separation is conceptually appropriate, the method is tested with two solvers, and the experiments cover six diverse problem families, including two described as real-world datasets.

Empirical promise: The reported Gurobi results show large runtime reductions on several families—76% on CFLP, 78% on OTS, 66% on MMCN, 88% on MVC, and 95% on MIS—while mean reported suboptimality remains low.
Presentation: The motivation and high-level pipeline are easy to understand, and the main figures communicate the speed–quality tradeoff effectively.

Limitations/ethics: The paper candidly acknowledges the cost of generating optimal training labels, its inability to extend the frontier of solvable instances, heterogeneous speedups, and vulnerability to distribution shift. No inherently problematic data or ethical issue is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—decisive issue: Lemma 4.2 is false by an off-by-one error. For example, with c=1 and n=1, it claims P[Z2≥Z1]≥1, whereas for iid continuous variables this probability is 1/2. Theorem 4.1 states the plausible n/(c+1) bound, but its proof concludes (n+1)/(c+1), and the calibration prescription explicitly chooses n using this incorrect stronger quantity. Consequently, the advertised 95% guarantee does not follow. With c=100 and the apparent choice n=95, the stated theorem only gives 95/101≈94.1%; with c=28 and n=27, it gives 27/29≈93.1%.

The left-inverse definition is itself incorrect: it assigns infinity when x exceeds sup f, even though the first threshold crossing should then occur immediately. Under the written definition, arbitrarily large thresholds make all calibration trajectories appear successful at infinite time, potentially rendering the supremum defining κ unbounded. Several inverse equivalences used in the proof also require careful treatment of equality, discontinuities, and attainment.

Theorem 5.1 does not justify its uniform-convergence step. A VC bound established separately for each fixed u is used after taking a supremum over all u without a union argument or analysis of the joint (κ,u)-indexed class. Theorem 5.2 similarly applies a concentration statement to the data-selected κ without explicitly invoking and proving the required uniform DKW argument. These results may be repairable, but the presented proofs are incomplete.

Core quantities are inconsistent. The true gap g is defined as a relative gap, whereas the learned target and squashing construction use the absolute difference U−z*. Section 5 defines s(θ,κ)=gθ(τ̂κ(θ))−z*(θ)/|z*(θ)|, which is not a sensible suboptimality expression. Section 6 then drops the squashing construction and writes ĝ=h(X). These inconsistencies make it unclear which quantity is actually trained, calibrated, and guaranteed.

The empirical evidence does not validate the headline reliability claim. At the target 0.1% tolerance, CP-GRB reaches only 88% correctness on MVC, while CP-COPT reaches 85% on GISP, 78.6% on OTS, and 80% on MMCN. Figure 4 instead switches to the looser 0.2% tolerance. A marginal conformal guarantee need not hold on one test split, but the paper repeatedly describes at-least-95% performance 'with high probability'; its sample-conditional theorem actually subtracts a potentially large O(1/√c) term.

The appendix statistics appear internally inconsistent. For example, OTS CP-COPT reports 78.6% of instances within 0.1%, mean suboptimality 0.15%, but standard deviation only 0.0032%; values this concentrated around 0.15% could not have 78.6% at or below 0.1%. Similar tensions occur elsewhere. This suggests a unit conversion, standard-error labeling, or reporting error that must be resolved before the evaluation can be trusted.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the promised code link is blank, and important details are missing, including solver versions and parameters, callback/sampling frequency, split identifiers and seeds, optimizer hyperparameters, threshold implementation, and inference overhead. The proposed weight w(t)∝1/y(t) is undefined when an optimal incumbent makes y(t)=0, with no numerical convention specified.

The evaluation disables presolve, restricts solvers to one thread and 1 GB, and provides no comparison under standard production configurations. Although settings are shared within each comparison, they may substantially inflate the apparent opportunity for early stopping and limit the practical significance of the reported speedups.

Presentation contains several consequential errors: the abstract and conclusion say five families although six are evaluated; the MVC results are duplicated under an erroneous 'Maximum vertex capacity' heading; and the paper alternates between 0.1% and 0.2% success criteria. These are more serious than cosmetic issues because they obscure what was actually tested.

The failure mode deserves more ethical discussion given the paper's motivating examples in robotics, power systems, and control. A distribution-level 5% failure rate is not a per-instance certificate and may be unsuitable for safety-critical deployment; distribution-shift detection and a fallback policy should be discussed. Overall, the idea is promising, but the central guarantee and experimental reporting require substantial correction before acceptance.

strengths: Originality/significance: Learning a distribution-specific early-stopping rule for an exact MIP solver, with trajectory-level conformal calibration, is a useful and reasonably novel direction. It is clearly distinguished from learning solver decisions or certifying an independent heuristic.

Soundness: The basic marginal conformal construction in Theorem 4.1 is intuitive and addresses repeated testing across callbacks by calibrating the first threshold-crossing event over complete trajectories.

Empirical scope: The evaluation covers six Distributional MIPLIB families, two solvers, simple learned and heuristic alternatives, solver-gap baselines, distribution-shift experiments, and calibration-size sensitivity. CP-GRB reports large runtime reductions on five families.
Presentation: The main motivation and pipeline are easy to follow, and the paper provides convergence plots and detailed tabular results rather than reporting only aggregate speedups.

Limitations/ethics: The paper honestly notes the cost of generating solved training instances, restriction to already-solvable families, variable speedups, and the iid assumption. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: The empirical results do not convincingly support the central 95%-success claim. At the stated 0.1% tolerance, CP-GRB attains only 88% correctness on MVC, while CP-COPT attains 85% on GISP, 78.6% on OTS, 80% on MMCN, and 91% on MIS. These substantial failures are dismissed as compatible with a probabilistic guarantee without confidence intervals, repeated calibrations, or diagnosis. Moreover, the repeated-calibration experiment reports mean coverage of only 92.7% and 92.8% for CFLP and GISP at c=100, despite the claimed marginal guarantee exceeding 95%.

Soundness: The sample-conditional theory has proof gaps. In Theorem 5.1, a fixed-u VC bound is taken uniformly over an uncountable range of u without controlling the joint class indexed by (kappa,u). In Theorem 5.2, a concentration inequality is applied directly to an event whose threshold kappa was selected from the same calibration data; a uniform argument over the nested threshold class is required but not supplied. Theorem 5.3 also writes an invalid equality that subtracts an absolute probability difference, although the intended lower bound may be repairable.

Method specification: The training objective weights observations by 1/y even though y becomes zero when an optimal incumbent is found, making the stated loss undefined. No clipping or regularization is specified. There are also inconsistent units: the theoretical gap is relative, whereas the network output and training target are expressed in absolute objective units and bounded by U-L.

Evaluation design: Presolve is disabled and Gurobi is set to MIPFocus=1, so the baseline is not representative of standard optimized solver use and may amplify the gap between finding and certifying a solution. Results against tuned/default solvers, stronger early-termination policies, and end-to-end overhead are missing. Figure 4 further evaluates 0.2%-optimality although calibration targets 0.1%, weakening its relevance to the headline claim.

Reproducibility: The promised code link is blank. Essential details such as optimizer hyperparameters, epochs, batch construction, feature normalization, callback sampling, random seeds, threshold-computation procedure, handling of infinite bounds and zero targets, and model-selection protocol are absent. Table 1 also lists 800 OTS training instances while stating that only 100 real-world OTS instances exist, without explaining the source or distribution of the training set.

Presentation: Several claims overstate the evidence, including saying the method maintains 0.1%-optimality with 95% probability while prominent reported test sets fall far below 95%. Figure 4's caption switches to 2epsilon, and uncertainty reporting and percentage units are inconsistent across tables. These issues obscure whether discrepancies arise from finite-sample variation, implementation errors, or reporting mistakes.

Overall: The early-stopping idea is promising and the marginal conformal construction may be salvageable, but unresolved proof gaps, observed coverage failures, and insufficient reproducibility directly affect the paper's central guarantee. These are acceptance-blocking rather than minor revisions.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: exact MIP solvers can find excellent incumbents long before certifying them. Calibrating an early-stopping rule for repeated, distributional solves could therefore be useful.

The trajectory-level conformal construction in Theorem 4.1 is an interesting contribution: it calibrates the first threshold-crossing event rather than treating every callback as an independent prediction, thereby addressing the sequential multiple-testing issue.

The evaluation covers six problem families, including two real-world datasets, and two commercial solvers. For Gurobi, the reported runtime reductions are substantial on five families while most returned solutions satisfy the target tolerance.

The appendices include simple-predictor baselines, alternative solver tolerances, calibration-size sensitivity, and distribution perturbations. The limitations section also honestly acknowledges training-data cost, problem-dependent speedups, and distributional assumptions.
The manuscript is generally organized and readable, and no material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: The basic optimality argument is not sound as stated. Section 3.3 claims (U-z*)/|z*| <= (U-L)/|L| solely from L <= z*, but this is false without additional sign or magnitude assumptions; for example, L=-2, z*=-1, U=1 gives 2 > 1.5. Consequently, the claim that the conventional stopping rule necessarily implies the paper's defined epsilon-optimality—and the framing built upon it—requires correction.

The predictor is inconsistently defined. Earlier sections treat g and g-hat as normalized relative gaps, whereas Section 4.2 defines g-hat in the absolute interval [0,U-L] and trains it against U-z*. This dimensional mismatch also makes one global absolute threshold sensitive to objective scaling, yet neither normalization nor scale robustness is studied.

The proposed training loss is undefined at important samples: w(t) is proportional to 1/y(t), while y(t)=U(t)-z* becomes zero once an optimal incumbent is found. No clipping, regularization, or exclusion rule is specified. The text also inconsistently declares h to be nonnegative while describing a final output unit that appears linear; if h is genuinely nonnegative, the sigmoid construction cannot predict less than half the certified gap.

The sample-conditional results are not adequately justified. In Theorem 5.1, a fixed-u VC bound is followed by a supremum over an uncountable set of u without establishing uniform control over u. Theorem 5.2 applies a concentration statement to an event whose threshold was selected from the same calibration sample without clearly invoking and proving the required uniform empirical-process result. These claims may be repairable using the nested score structure, but the supplied proofs do not establish the displayed results.

The empirical evidence does not consistently support the headline interpretation. Although alpha=0.05, observed epsilon-coverage is only 88% for CP-GRB on MVC and is 85%, 78.6%, 80%, and 91% for CP-COPT on GISP, OTS, MMCN, and MIS. Marginal conformal validity can coexist with poor coverage for one fixed calibration set, but the abstract and conclusion do not clearly distinguish this from a practically useful 95% conditional guarantee.

Reported statistics are internally inconsistent. For example, CP-GRB CFLP suboptimality is 0.015% +/- 0.00028 in Table 5 but 0.018% +/- 0.037 in Table 11; analogous discrepancies occur for other families. This suggests inconsistent runs, incorrect standard-deviation scaling, or reporting errors and prevents confident interpretation of the evaluation.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the promised code link is blank, and essential choices such as optimizer learning rate, epochs, batching, random seeds, callback sampling, discretization, feature preprocessing, weight regularization, and exact split construction are omitted. It is also unclear whether neural-inference/callback overhead is included and how true optima are established for instances subject to the 600-second limit.

The distribution-shift experiment does not validate the stated TV-robustness claim because the total-variation distance induced by the generator perturbation is neither computed nor bounded. Observing little degradation under an unquantified perturbation cannot be connected to Theorem 5.3.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional. The main novelty is applying conformal calibration to a solver stopping trajectory; the underlying predictor-plus-calibration approach is close in spirit to prior conformal validation of learned MIP heuristics, and the paper does not sufficiently isolate what new technical difficulty the stopping formulation resolves beyond the order-statistic argument.

strengths: Originality: The paper presents a compelling combination of learned solver-state trajectories and conformal calibration. Calibrating the first threshold-crossing time addresses repeated testing across callbacks and is more interesting than simply attaching uncertainty to independent point predictions.

Significance: The problem is important because MIP solvers can find strong incumbents long before certifying them. Reported Gurobi speedups are substantial on five families (approximately 66–95%), and experiments span six families, two solvers, synthetic and real-world data, and several heuristic and solver-tolerance baselines.

Presentation: The main motivation, algorithmic pipeline, and distinction between marginal and sample-conditional guarantees are generally explained clearly. Figures and tables are legible, and the convergence-curve analysis helps establish when early stopping can be useful.
The empirical split between training, calibration, and test data is conceptually appropriate, and the predictor is evaluated through actual solver callbacks rather than an offline proxy alone.

The limitations section candidly identifies the expensive requirement for solved training instances, the method's inability to expand the tractable frontier, family-dependent speedups, and sensitivity to distribution shift. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: The coverage experiments conflict with the paper's central guarantee and are not reconciled. Table 16 reports mean coverage of only 88.8–91.4% for c=20, although Theorem 4.1's prescribed n=20 gives marginal coverage of at least 20/21=95.24%. For c=100, CFLP and GISP achieve only 92.7% and 92.8% across 100 calibration repetitions, well below the promised level. Moreover, no valid n exists for alpha=0.05 when c=5 or c=10, yet results are reported without specifying an alternative procedure. These systematic discrepancies suggest that the implementation, theorem, or reported experiment does not match.

The main test results reinforce this concern: CP-COPT reaches only 85.0% on GISP, 78.6% on OTS, 80.0% on MMCN, and 91.0% on MIS, while CP-GRB reaches only 88.0% on MVC. Individual fixed-split deviations are possible under marginal conformal validity, but the paper repeatedly describes 95% performance more strongly than the guarantee supports, and the repeated-calibration results make a chance explanation unconvincing.

The additional theoretical results contain gaps. Theorem 5.1 obtains a bound for each fixed suboptimality level u and then takes a supremum over the continuum of u without establishing uniform convergence for the joint class indexed by both kappa and u. Theorem 5.3 also writes an equality subtracting an absolute probability difference that is only an inequality in general. These issues undermine the advertised sample-conditional theory, even if the basic split-conformal argument may be repairable.

Several definitions are internally inconsistent. The true gap g is defined as a relative gap, but the network is trained against the unnormalized quantity U-z*, while the manuscript continues to call its output an estimate of g. The stated left-inverse assigns infinity when x exceeds sup f, whereas the first time f(t)≤x should then normally be zero. The loss weight proportional to 1/y is singular once an optimal incumbent is found, with no stabilization described.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The displayed code link is blank, and essential details such as preprocessing and normalization, callback sampling, batching, epochs, learning rate, random seeds, numerical handling of zero targets and infinite bounds, exact calibration-quantile implementation, and inference overhead are absent. Table 1 is also contradictory: OTS is said to have only 100 instances in total, but lists 800 training instances plus 28 calibration and 72 test instances, leaving possible data reuse or leakage unresolved.

The practical comparison is weakened by disabling presolve and using a nondefault Gurobi MIPFocus setting without evaluating against a well-tuned/default production solver. Some simple alternatives outperform the LSTM in time on CFLP, GISP, and MVC, while relaxed native MIPGap settings dominate it on several time-quality tradeoffs. A broader Pareto-style comparison and ablations of the learned features/model would better establish the LSTM's added value.

The distributional assumptions need more careful treatment. The authors state that repeated iid resampling is impossible for the real OTS and MMCN datasets, yet invoke iid conformal guarantees for them. The shift study reports only mean suboptimality, not coverage or an estimate of total-variation distance, so it does not empirically validate the robustness guarantee.

Some statistical reporting is unclear: the units of standard deviations in the suboptimality tables appear inconsistent with the percentage-valued means, uncertainty over speedups is not quantified, and Figure 4 switches from the calibrated 0.1% target to a 0.2% evaluation threshold. Overall, the idea is promising, but unresolved contradictions surrounding the central coverage claim prevent acceptance in its current form.
